Saukat Ali Khan, Advocate, instructed by A. Baset Majumder, Advocate-on-Record ----- for the Appellants
Md. Rafiqul Islam, Advocate, instructed by B.C. Panday, Advocate-on-Record ----- for the Respondents 1-32 & 34-38
parties:
Mokarram Ali & others
Vs.
Abdul Samad & others
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J.:- This appeal by special leave by the defendants in a partition suit arises from the judgment of the High Court dated July 26, 1976 in First Appeal No. 6 of 1964.

2. The appeal raises an important question of law, in that whether the doctrine of res judicata as provided in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has got any application in the case where two suits, one title suit instituted by the appellants and the other partition suit instituted by the respondents making the plaintiffs of the title suit as defendants in respect of the selfsame property, having been disposed of by one judgment, dismissing the title suits and decreeing the partition suit, and the plaintiffs in the title suit preferring appeal against the decree in the partition suit, the decree in the title suit operates as res judicata in the appeal.

3. Facts, in short, necessary for disposal of the appeal may be stated thus : two suits being Title Suit No. 55 of 1961/ 80 of 1962 and Partition Suit No. 25 of 1961/79 of 1962 between the same parties were heard analogously and disposed of by one judgment and separate decrees. The appellants instituted Title Suit No. 55 of 1961 on February 17, 1961 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Comilla which on transfer to the court of Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Comilla was renumbered as Title Suit No. 80 of 1962, for confirmation of their possession and for a declaration of their title that the property described in schedule (1) to the plaint were the self-acquired property of Kala Gazi and not of the father of Kala Gazi as claimed by the plaintiffs of the portion suit. Respondents 1 to 23 instituted Partition Suit No. 25 of 1961 on February 29, 1961 in the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge which on transfer to the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Comilla was renumbered as Partition Suit No. 79 of 1962. The case of the said plaintiffs, inter alia, is that all the lands described in the schedules 1 to 4 to the plaint belonged to two brothers, Ashok Gazi and Kala Gazi in equal shares. Ashok Gazi died leaving behind two sons Jinnat Ali and Ashraf Ali who inherited 4 annas share each in the case land. Thereafter Jinnat Ali died leaving behind the plaintiffs 1 to 17 and Ashraf Ali died leaving behind the plaintiffs 18 to 23. Thus the plaintiffs 1 to 23 collectively inherited 8 annas share in the entire case land. On the other hand Kala Gazi died leaving behind two sons Fazle Ali, predecessor of defendants 1 to 3, and Tamizuddin predecessor of defendants 4 to 8. Thus the defendants 1 to 8 collectively inherited 8 annas share in the entire suit property. The partition suit was contested by the defendants 1, 4, 5 and 6 by filing a joint written statement. There was no dispute with regard to the lands described in schedules 2, 3 and 4. The dispute was in respect of the property described in schedule 1 only. The defendants claimed that the property described in schedule were the self-acquired property of their predecessor Kala Gazi who acquired the same by a patta dated 4th Flagon, 1293 B.S. Both the suits were disposed of by one judgment dismissing the title suit and decreeing the partition suit on the finding that the schedule property in the partition suit was not the self-acquired property of Kala Gazi but belonged to the father of Kala Gazi. The appellants who were the defendants in the partition suit filed an appeal against the decree passed in the partition suit but they did not file any appeal against the decree dismissing their title suit. At the hearing of the appeal the learned Judges of the High Court accepted the contention of the respondents that the question regarding the appellants claim to schedule 1 property on the ground that the properties were the self-acquired property of Kala Gazi, could not be agitated in the appeal, because, the appellants were estopped from raising this question, inasmuch as, the issue was decided in the title suit itself, wherein it was held by the trial court that the properties of schedule 1 to the plaint in the title suit were not the self-acquired property of Kala Gazi but were the properties belonged to the common ancestor of the parties, namely, father of Kala Gazi. On this finding the appeal was dismissed.

4. In this back ground leave was granted to examine the question whether doctrine of res judicata as provided in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has any application to such a case, that is, the judgment in the title suit in the absence of any appeal therefrom, being a decision in the former suit within the meaning of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, operates as res judicata in the appeal from the decree in the partition suit.

5. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants submitted that the learned Judges of the High Court on clear misconception about the provision of res judicata as contained in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure wrongly held that the appellants were not entitled to agitate the question of title to schedule property in the appeal from the decree in the partition suit. In support of this contention he argued that both the title suit and the partition suit involving substantially the same disputed question as to whether schedule property was the self-acquired property of the appellants' predecessor and both the suits having been heard together and disposed of by one judgment, the learned Judges committed an error of procedure in not allowing the appellants to agitate the said question, which being practically the common question in both the suits, was sought to be raised in appeal from the partition decree. According to the learned Counsel the decision in the title suit cannot be taken to be the decision in the "former suit" as contemplated in section 11.

6. Mr. Saukat Ali Khan relied upon a decision of a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court in the case of Pramatha Nath Chaudhury etc. v. Rai Dwarka Nath Chakraborti Chaudhury Bahadur etc. (1). Relying on the authority of this decision the learned Counsel submitted that the test of res judicata in such cases tried analogously is whether the Judge did apply his mind to the issue involved in the suits separately or whether there has been in fact one trial, one finding and one decision. According to him in the instant case the issues were framed separately but issue No. 4 in the title suit relating to the question whether the suit land was the self-acquired property of Kala Gazi, was considered along with issue Nos. 1 and 2 of the partition suit, that is, whether the plaintiffs have any right, title and interest in the suit land. The learned Counsel referred to relevant portion of the judgment to show how the issues have been considered and disposed of. The Trial Court concluded as follows:

"All these considerations lead to the conclusion that this first schedule property was acquired by Ashok and Kala Gazi together while they were joint that the document was taken in the name of Kala Gazi."

With reference to the above finding the learned Counsel submitted that there being one finding and one decision in the two suits, the question cannot be treated being "substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties", and as such the learned Judges wrongly applied the doctrine of res judicata in the instant case and thereby depriving the appellants from getting decision of the Appellate Court on the question.

7. For proper appreciation of the decision in P.L.R. 7 Dacca at page 209 short statement of facts of the case is necessary. Originally 344 rent suits involving decision on the common issues were tried analogously and the Trial Court delivered one common judgment which disposed of all the rent suits. Against the judgment 22 appeals were preferred by some of the tenant defendants and preformat-defendants in 22 rent suits. The appeals arising out of the common judgment and raising common points for decision were consolidated and disposed of by one judgment by the lower Appellate Court, who reversed the judgment of the Trial Court and set aside the decrees passed in the suits which were under appeal. The lower Appellate Court held that the appeals were barred by res judicata. Against the appellate judgment 17 appeals were taken to the High Court in second appeal by the plaintiffs. 15 of these appeals being ready for hearing, on the prayer of the parties were heard analogously and disposed of by the same judgment. On behalf of the plaintiff-appellants was canvassed that the appeals preferred by some of the tenant defendants against the judgment of the Trial Court were barred by res judicata. Firstly, because, no appeal was preferred against the judgment in the remaining suits wherein issues we e common and finally decided upon and adjudicated; and secondly, because, in the proceedings started in Mymensingh to execute a decree passed by the Calcutta High Court in favour of the plaintiffs, the objection as to the validity of the determination of the lease was raised and adjudicated upon, the defendant respondents were estopped from raising that issue in these appeals.

8. The learned Judges in considering the question reviewed a large number of decisions of different High Courts wherein the question whether the decision in the cases from which no appeal has been preferred operates as res judicata has been considered. The learned Judges particularly on the authority of the Lahore Full Bench in the case of Mt. Lachmi v. Mt Bhulli, (1) held that the appeals which were heard by the Additional District Judge, and also the appeals before the High Court were neither hit by the provisions of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure nor barred by the general principles of res judicata. While taking this view the learned Judges observed as follows:-

"One broad feature stares us in the case, namely, that neither according to the terms of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure nor upon general principles, one can urge that the very same judgment will bar an appeal against it. It has been consistently laid down in all leading decisions that it is the judgment, and not the decree passed thereof which attracts principles of res judicata."

Let me examine whether the test applied in Pramatha Nath Chaudhury's case and also in the Lahore Full Bench case is applicable to the facts of the instant case. It has been already noted above that two suits were instituted in the same Court being Title Suit No. 55 of 1961 and Partition Suit No. 25 of 1961; and on transfer to the court of Subordinate Judge, Second Court; Comilla, the suits were renumbered as Title Suit No. 55 of 1961/80 of 1962 and Partition Suit No. 79 of 196/25 of 19612. The plaintiffs in the former suit were defendants in the later suit and the plaintiffs in the later suit were defendants in the former suit; and that both the suits were heard analogously and disposed of by one judgment; title suit was dismissed and the partition suit was decreed. Partition suit was filed by the descendants of Ashok Gazi. One of the issues framed in Title Suit filed by defendants 1 to 8 of the Partition Suit is—

Issue No. 4 Is the suit land self-acquired property of Kala Gazi and is the story of permissive possession of Ashok Gazi and after him his heirs true?

Two of the issues framed in the Partition Suit are—

Issue No. 5 Have the plaintiffs any right, title and interest in the suit land?

Issue No. 6 Are the plaintiffs entitled to get any decree for partition, if so, what is the share of the plaintiffs?

9. Contest in both the suits was with regard to the first schedule lands and there was no controversy with regard to the lands of other 3 schedules. Defendants in the partition suit who were the plaintiffs in the title suit claimed the entire first schedule property with the exception of plots 578 and 579 measuring 93 decimals as belonging exclusively to them. With regard to the first schedule property their case is that the lands comprising of five plots measuring 4.97 acres was acquired by a patta dated 4th Falgoon, 1293 B.S. by Kala Gazi alone and it was his exclusive property; and that Kala Gazi out of sympathy allowed his brother Ashok Gazi to possess 93 decimals of plots 578 and 579. The plaintiffs in the partition suit who were the defendants in the title suit claimed that all the lands of "Ka", "Kha" and "Ga" schedules of the title suit were the ejmali properties of their predecessors Jinnat Ali, Ashraf Ali, Fazle Ali and Tamizuddin in equal shares. The trial Court accepted the case of the plaintiffs in the partition suit that the first schedule property was acquired by Ashok Gazi and Kala Gazi together while they were joint but the document was taken in the name of Kala Gazi, and arrived at the following conclusion:-

"So following from the above conclusions the 4th issue of the title suit is answered in the negative and on the fifth issue of the partition suit it is found that the plaintiffs have their half share in the lands of all the four schedules."

On the above finding the partition suit was decreed in preliminary form on contest with necessary directions, and the title suit was dismissed. The appeal preferred against the decree passed in partition suit was dismissed on the ground that the appeal was barred by operation of the decision in the title suit as no appeal from that decree was preferred.

10. The main object of the doctrine of res judicata is to prevent multiplicity of suits and interminable disputes between litigants. There is some controversy on the question of application of the principle of res judicata to a case arising out of similar situation. This question was elaborately examined by Sir Ashutosh Mookerjee in the case of Isup Ali v. Gour Chandra Deb, (1). Facts in that case are as follows: A, B and C brought a suit against D for recovery of possession of certain land. A few days later, D and his brothers instituted against A, B and C a suit for establishment of their title to the home-stead portion of the property involved in the suit. The suits were jointly tried together and disposed of by one judgment. The former suit was dismissed but the latter suit was decreed. The plaintiffs in the first suit preferred an appeal annexing both the decrees with the memorandum of appeal, which, however, set out the name of D alone as the respondent. Objection was raised on the maintainability of the appeal on the ground that the appeal was barred by the decision in the subsequent suit between the same parties and others. The contention was accepted on the ground that the decision could not be collaterally attacked or implicitly ignored in appeal.

11. Mookerjee, J. in delivering the judgment referred to a decision in Balkishan v. Kishan Lal, (2) wherein Mahmood, J. observed that the doctrine of res judicata, so far as it relates to prohibiting the retrial of an issue, must refer not to the date of commencement of the litigation, but to the time when the Judge is called upon to decide the issue; and the rule is not limited to the courts of the first instance, it applies equally to the procedure of the first and second Appellate Courts. Mookerjee, J. found himself in complete agreement with the exposition of the law given by Mahmood, J. in the following passage:-

"It seems to me that the main object of the doctrine of res judicata is to prevent multiplicity of the suits and interminable dispute between litigants ne autem lites immortals essent, dum litigantes mortales sunt.

This being so, the doctrine, so far as it relates to prohibiting the retrial of an issue, must refer not to the date of commencement of the litigation, but to the time when the Judge is called upon to decide the issue. For even in cases where the Judge has commenced the trial of an issue which is also an issue in a pending litigation, a final judgment pronounced meanwhile in such previous litigation, by a competent court (the identity of parties and other conditions being satisfied), should operate as res judicata, preventing the Judge dealing with the later litigation from adjudicating differently. If this is not done, it seems to me that the evil against which res judicata aims would not be removed and the doctrine itself would be defeated."

This view of Mahmood, J. has been reaffirmed by the Allahabad High Court in several later decisions.

12. A different view was taken in some earlier decisions of Madras High Court and Bombay High Court, for instance in Podiananda Velan v. Vaithinatha Sastrial, (1) Avanasi v. Nachammal, (2) and Govind v. Dhond, (3). A view was taken that decree unappeased did not operate as a bar, so as to preclude the appellate Court from dealing with the decree appealed against, because, it was said, the doctrine of res judicata has no application when the very object of the appeal, in substance, if not in form, is to get rid of the decision which is appealed from. According to this view, it would lead to startling result, if courts were to hold that an appellate Tribunal is precluded from dealing with a question which comes before it on appeal, because an inferior court upon the same facts, but in a case other than the case under appeal, had given a decision which had not been appealed against at the same time as the decision in the case under appeal. The above decision, however, stand superseded by the Explanation II of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. In a later case a Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Zaharia v. Debia (4) stated the rule with approval of the view taken in the earlier decisions of that Court as referred to above. In that case M and Z filed suits for pre-emption in respect of the sale each claiming right of pre-emption preferential to that of the other. The suit of M was decreed but that of Z was dismissed. Z appealed from the decree of its own suit but not from the decree in the suit brought by M which became final before Z's appeal was decided. It was held in that case that the doctrine of res judicata applied and Z's appeal was barred.

13. So far available, the leading case on the point is the case of Mt. Lachhmi v. Mt. Bhulli, (5) In this case a Full Bench of the Lahore High Court discussed extensively the principles governing the doctrine of res judicata. Two widows A and B were jointly in possession of certain laid. Each sued the other for declaration that she (plaintiff) was the exclusive owner of that land, and that the other (defendant) had no right in it of any kind. Both the suits were disposed of by a single judgment which decided that A was the owner, but that B was entitled to hold possession of half of the land in lieu of maintenance. A separate decree was drawn up in each suit declaring the rights of the respective plaintiff according to that decision. B appealed against one of these decree only, namely, the decree given in the suit in which she was the plaintiff. It was held (by the majority judgment) that the decree in the other suit cannot bar B's appeal. With regard to the question of analogous hearing of suits Tek Chand, J. dealt with the question at length. The learned Judge, inter alia, observed:

“The essence of the rule seems to me to be that the two proceedings should be so independent of each other that the trial of one cannot be confused with the trial of the other. (Where two suits, having a common issue are, by consent of parties or by order of the court, tried together the evidence being written in one record, and both suits disposed of by a single judgment, can it be said that there have been two distinct and independent trials? There being but one finding and one judgment on what principle can the hearing of the appeal in which this finding and this judgment are under consideration be barred, merely because no appeal has been filed in the connected suit which was disposed of by that very judgment ? There has been in substance, as well as in form but one verdict and I venture to think, it will be a travesty of justice to stifle the hearing of the appeal against such a judgment on the ground that the findings contained in it operate as res judicata. In such case there can be no question of the successful party being vexed twice over the same matter, nor does the hearing of the appeal in any way, militate against any rule of public policy which required that there must be an end of litigation. There is not only nothing here to attract the principles underlying the rule of res judicata, but, on the other hand it seems to me that the acceptance of such a plea in such circumstances would strike at the very root of the basic conception of the doctrine, which requires that a pasty must have at least one fair trial of the issue resulting in a decision by the court of ultimate appeal as allowed by the law for the time being in force".

The Supreme Court of India in the case of Narahari v. Shankar, (1) has noted the above noted decision of the Lahore Full Bench in Mt. Lachhmi v. Mt. Bhulli and it has been approved. Naik, J. observed as follows:

"As has been observed by Tek Chand J. in his learned judgment in Mt. Lachhmi v. Mt. Bhulli mentioned above, the determining factor is not the decree but the matter in controversy. As he puts it later in his judgment, the estoppel is not created by the decree, but it can only be created by the judgment. The question of res judicata arises only when there are two suits it has been held that a decision given simultaneously cannot be a decision in the former suit. When there is only one suit, the question of res judicata does not arise at all, and in the present case, both the decrees are in the same case, and based on the same judgment, and the matter decided concerns the entire suit, as such, there is no question of the application of the principle of res judicata. The same judgment cannot remain effective just because it was appealed against with a different number or a copy of it was attached to a different appeal. The two decrees in substance are one."

14. On the authority of the decisions noted above the learned Judges held that the appeals which were heard by the Additional District Judge and also the appeals before the High Court were neither hit by the provisions of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure nor barred by the general principles of res judicata.

<u>15. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan on the authority of this decision vigorously argued that the first appeal preferred by the appellants was not barred by the-decision in the title suit not appealed from. According to him the principles of res judicata have no application in such a case.</u>

<u>Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as under:</u>

<u>"11. Res judicata.—No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such court".</u>

<u>The meaning and scope of the expression "former suit" has been clarified by introducing Explanation I to section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 1908. The expression "former suit" contemplates a suit which has been decided earlier than the suit in question, irrespective of the fact of the suit being instituted prior or after the institution of the suit in question. If two suits are filed one after another and the same question is in controversy, the decision in the later suit if given earlier operates as res judicata. For instance, the defendant in a suit for ejectment takes the plea that the plaintiff has no title. Pending disposal of the suit a third person claiming title to the suit property by instituting a suit gets his title established. The decision operates as res judicata to the suit for ejectment. The principle however is not applicable in a case where several suits involving common issues between the same parties are disposed of by one judgment, decrees being passed in each, but one decree is appealed from, the matter decided in the decrees not appealed from does not operate as res judicata to the appeal. Application of the doctrine of res judicata to a suit or appeal preferred therefrom is dependent on the nature of the suit and the common issues framed in the suits. If the suits are connected and the issue framed therein is also common so as to constitute virtually a single suit on the issue, in such a case the decree not appealed from will not operate as res judicata.</u>

16. The decision in the case of Pramatha Nath Chowdhury etc. v. Rai Dwarka Nath Chakraborti Chowdhury Bahadur etc., (1) however, does not lend support to the arguments of Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In the reported case, as have been noted above 344 rent suits involving decision on common issues were tried analogously and disposed of by one judgment. Of course, separate decrees were made and kept in the file of each suit, 22 appeals were preferred by some of the tenant-defendants and proforma-defendants. At the hearing of the appeals objection was taken on the ground that the appeals were barred by res judicata, because, no appeals were preferred against the decrees passed in the other suits. The question was decided by the Additional District Judge in favour of the plaintiffs that the appeals preferred by defendants were barred by res judicata and on second appeal the High Court reversed the decision on the finding that the appeals were not barred by res judicata. We may not approve of all the reasons given for reversing the decision of the lower Appellate Court but the conclusion, in the facts and circumstances of that case, cannot be said to have not been correctly arrived. All the suits being rent suits and the issues touching the question of relationship of landlord and tenants and the liability of the tenant defendants to pay rent claimed by the landlord in the suits being common in all the suits, the decrees not appealed from could not operate as res judicata.

17. In the instant case the position is different. Title Suit No. 80 of 1962 was instituted by the present appellants on 17-2-61 and the defendants of the suit instituted Partition Suit No. 25 of 1961 on 29-2-61 for Partition of lands which of course includes amongst others the suit lands of the title suit. The question as to whether the properties in dispute were the exclusive properties of Kala Gazi was the principal issue for adjudication in the title suit, which issue might have been incidentally considered in the partition suit, but there was no scope for deciding the question of title in the partition suit. In disposing of the partition suit, the issue on the question of title might have been examined incidentally, but from this it cannot be said that the issue relating to title has been decided by the judgment so far it relates to the partition suit.

<u>18. In the title suit the decision was that the suit property did not belong to Kala Gazi alone and the suit was dismissed. In that view of the matter although in the title suit and the partition suit some common issues were framed, and both the suits were disposed of by one judgment, the decision of the court on the question of title cannot be said to have been given in the partition suit also, because, the issue was not directly and substantially in issue therein. Obviously the property was partitioned treating the property of 'Ka' schedule as the property jointly acquired by Ashok Gazi and Kala Gazi. So, the decree passed in the title suit not appealed from operates as res judicata to the appeal from the decree in the partition suit. The decision on the question of title to the Schedule 1 property given in the title suit could not be collaterally attacked in the appeal from the decree in the Partition Suit.</u>

<u>19. The doctrine of res judicata, so far as it relates to prohibiting retrial of an issue refers not to the date of commencement of the suit but to the time when the Judge is called upon to decide the issue. The rule is not limited to the court of first instance, but it also applies to the proceedings of the first and second Appellate Courts. The main object of the doctrine of res judicata is to prevent multiplicity of suits and interminable dispute between litigants. The question of title cannot be said to be substantially in issue in the partition suit, but it was so in the title suit. So, the question of title cannot be said to be common in the two suits. From the judgment of the trial Court it appears that the trial court dealt with 4th issue of title suit separately and answered in the negative. And the 5th issue of the partition was answered separately. It has been found that the plaintiffs have their half share in the lands of all the four schedules. The decision on the question of title given in the title suit became final in the absence of any appeal therefrom. It could not be reopened in the appeal from the decree in the partition suit. The High Court has taken the correct view in the matter. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs.</u>

End.
